blocks.title: Know what a package does before you install it
blocks.description: Drop an APK, IPA, DEX, shared library, executable or archive into the workspace and get a readable verdict: what it is, what it asks for, what it hides, and how much it deserves your trust.

items.title: Format-aware facts
items.description: One pass recognises Android packages and bundles, iOS apps, ELF, PE, Mach-O, raw DEX and plain archives, then reports architecture, entry point, size, entropy and SHA-256.

items.title: Manifest and permission review
items.description: Reads the binary AndroidManifest inside the APK: package identity, SDK range, debuggable and backup flags, exported components and every requested permission.

items.title: Native hardening checks
items.description: Flags writable+executable segments, executable stacks, missing PIE or NX, packer signatures and stripped tooling — the differences that decide how hard a library is to attack.

items.title: Evidence, not guesses
items.description: Runtime-loading, shell execution, reflection, weak crypto and credential-shaped strings are reported with the exact strings and offsets that triggered them.

items.title: One score you can defend
items.description: Each rule carries a severity and a weight, so the 0-100 risk score and A-E grade can be traced back to named rule ids instead of a black box.

items.title: Reports that leave the app
items.description: Copy the markdown, or save markdown or JSON through the system dialog to attach to a review, a ticket or an internal security note.

showcase.assistant_reply: Three exported components with no permission guard, a DexClassLoader that unpacks the real code at runtime, and SMS / location / contacts permissions.

blocks.content:
**Why 62 (grade D)**

- `apk.exported-component` · High — 3 activities and services are exported with no permission guard.
- `apk.dynamic-loading` · High — `DexClassLoader` appears in the DEX, so the real logic is unpacked at runtime.
- `apk.dangerous-permission` · Medium — requests `READ_SMS`, `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION` and `READ_CONTACTS`.

The package also has no v2/v3 signature, only the legacy `META-INF` one. Re-download it from the official channel; if you must keep analysing it, dump the runtime-loaded dex first and review that code instead.

items.title: Open the Hanshuang Pojia tab
items.description: In a project conversation, add the panel from the activity tab bar. It lists the packages and binaries already in the workspace folder.

items.title: Pick any sample, from anywhere
items.description: Drop a file on the panel or click Open local file — it does not have to live inside the project. The bytes are copied into .hanshuang/samples in the workspace first, then analysed locally; anything above 32 MiB is refused before the copy. Nothing is uploaded and nothing is executed.

items.title: Read the report
items.description: Risk score, the findings that drove it, manifest facts and per-section details. Switch between Summary and Full, then copy or save the report.

blocks.content: The activity-bar tab is now a fourteen-page workbench: Workbench, Guide, Documents, Samples, Findings, Strings, Disassembly, Manifest, Entropy, Signature, Compare, Self check, Reports and Settings. Every page reads the same report, so a sample you analyse once stays inspectable from every angle — including a report-to-report diff of two builds. Two pages stand on their own: Disassembly walks the sample's own executable sections, ranks candidate functions and renders one at a time as a control-flow listing in summary, branches-only or full density, cut at a character budget; Documents renders the 334 bundled field write-ups, manuals, tool docs and case studies the plugin ships byte for byte, with in-memory title search and on-demand full-text search, each body loaded as its own build chunk. Purple buttons send an English prompt to the conversation, and a report produced by the agent in chat appears back in the panel with a "from chat" marker. Settings can switch analysis mode, disable individual rules and change scan resolution; storage is optional and the panel degrades to session-only memory when the host has not granted it.

Code-level questions go through the agent: `list_code_symbols` reads ELF, PE and Mach-O symbol and export tables, `disassemble_range` sweeps an AArch64 or x86 byte range, `search_dex_symbols` finds classes, methods and strings in a DEX or APK, and `diff_binaries` shows what changed between two builds. Every listing is a linear sweep with file offsets - never decompiled source, and never a claim about what runs.

If radare2, jadx or apktool are already on this machine, the agent can borrow them instead of approximating: `probe_environment` reports which of the fourteen declared executables (r2 / rabin2 / radiff2 / rasm2 / rahash2 / rax2 / jadx / apktool / java / adb / apksigner / zipalign / frida / frida-ps) actually answer and with which version; `install_toolchain` turns the gaps into the exact install command for this platform, filtered to the goal at hand — apk, native, firmware, dynamic or full — and the plugin never runs it, you do; `run_radare` covers headers, full string scans, the analysed function list, disassembly, pseudo-C, cross references, assemble/disassemble and binary diff; `decompile_android` turns an APK into Java sources or smali next to it and then searches that tree without loading whole files. Nothing is downloaded or installed, every call is a single executable with an argument vector, and the command channel is read-only - writes, shells, the debugger and project commands are refused. When a binary is missing the answer says which one and how to install it; when the host refuses the channel it says that instead of pretending the engine answered. The write-up lands where the case lives: `init_task` lays out `samples/`, `exports/` and `reports/`, and `write_assessment_report` typesets the four-section assessment into `reports/`, leaving a section you did not supply explicitly unsupplied instead of inventing a conclusion for it.

The bundled agent document carries the workbench kit 2.0 protocol as its fifth part: lab mode entered with `lab：` and left with `退出实验`, the deployment and verification board driven by `setup/verify.ps1 -Detailed`, knowledge-base-first recon, and the `seep` (23 MCP tools) / `ida` (~243) matrix with its Radare2 fallback table. Since 2.1 the kit's skill library ships with it - 165 files, 2.4 MB, byte-identical to the upstream tree, routed by path from the protocol. It is payload and documentation, not a dependency: the panel and the local radare2 / jadx tools work without the kit, and nothing here is installed behind your back.

This is static-first triage, not proof of safety. Android signature digests are read as structured fields — run `apksigner verify --print-certs` in your shell when the verdict matters; packed or encrypted code is flagged by `native.packed` and unpacking is the documented next step (`agent/skills/apkseep/references/advanced-unpacking.md`), not a dead end; behaviour that only shows up at runtime stays invisible to a static pass, so reach for a Frida run when the listing runs out. Treat a low score as "nothing obvious", not as an approval. Two hard limits come from the host, not the plugin: the engine only reads files the host is willing to open, and at most 32 MiB per file. Samples from anywhere else are still fine — the panel copies the bytes into .hanshuang/samples inside the workspace first, so the original stays untouched and its own location never becomes a limit.

Install this from the marketplace rather than from a downloaded package. The host records where an ability came from, and it never overwrites one source with another: if you already installed a build by hand, adding the newer one stops at "the same ability id is already installed from another source". Remove the hand-installed copy under My Abilities first, then install here — from then on upgrades follow the marketplace by themselves.
